en: The Sūtra on Governing the Mind Spoken by the Buddha;
the translator’s name is lost, now appended to the Western Jin Records.
The Buddha said: “Once one has fully practiced *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) according to the Dharma, and wishes to study in successive stages, it is as follows:”

As the Buddha has taught, one attains clarity while remaining in the world; as when the moon rises and stands upon the shadows, so too does the body stand and the mind stand, and it is the same whether sitting or reclining.
Once a bhikṣu has established his mind, he will thus find benefit in both the preceding and subsequent moments;
once there is such benefit in the preceding and subsequent moments, he will no longer perceive the mind as strange or anomalous.
Having stilled the mind, one also guards against the six sense-decadences;
guarding them constantly without ceasing, one then knows the unconditioned body.

If one has the intention to always guard the body, and brings it to rest so as not to desire, nor to desire existence, nor to doubt existence, nor to doubt non-existence, then by practicing step-by-step according to what was doubted, one will quickly attain liberation from birth and death.
If one’s mind is startled into awareness, knowing that concentration is joyful and pure, and if one contemplates the Dharma from time to time, one can transcend old age and sickness.

Thus, by being startled at the prospect of illness, the practitioner on the path of diligence brings about the severance of the fetters of birth and aging within their own mind; they can attain the end of suffering in this very life. Having been alerted, one listens; having been asleep, one awakens. Being alert is superior to lying down; for one who is alert, there is no fear.
Having already applied diligence to overcome sleep, one studies day and night; having sought the ambrosia, one then attains the extinction of suffering.

When a person possesses such benefit, they take refuge in the Buddha; during the middle watch of the night, they constantly keep the Buddha in mind. Having awakened to awakening, the disciples of the Buddha are always thus.

If, during the middle watch of the night, one constantly contemplates the Dharma, the Saṅgha is likewise, the practice of the precepts is likewise, generosity is likewise, the protection of the body is likewise, the practice of dhyāna is likewise, non-injury toward others is likewise, concentration of mind is likewise, and emptiness is likewise; having already awakened, one is able to awaken—thus the disciples of the Buddha are always thus, provided they do not fall into discursive thought during the middle [watch].
He asked: "What is meant by 'immediately knowing the unconditioned body'?
The Master said:
"Mud is the unconditioned body.
"What is sequential practice? "It refers to that which has been reached;
one should immediately eliminate it, and then eliminate it in succession—this is called sequential practice."
"What is the practice of observing phenomena at their respective times?
It means that when the six sense bases arise, one should immediately perform an analytical reckoning; this is called the practice of observing phenomena at their respective times."
“What is the practitioner’s own intention?

It means that when teaching others to be diligent, one must first practice it oneself; guarding one’s body and guarding one’s mind, one performs meritorious deeds for oneself. Because the merit of the heavens has not yet been fulfilled, one guards one’s own merit until it is complete, and then attains dhyāna.”
The Sūtra on Governing the Mind Spoken by the Buddha.
